intro: Games travel. Long ago, people in Mexico bounced rubber balls on stone courts. People in China kicked a leather ball. Native nations of North America played lacrosse. Later, ships and teachers carried soccer, basketball and baseball to new lands.
Some sports need a very different room. Wrestlers use a padded mat. Boxers use a roped square. Fencers use a long, thin strip. Judo began on straw mats at a school in Tokyo in 1882.
In this unit you will learn where games began and how they moved. You will name the room each sport needs. You will put real dates in order.
bigQuestion: How do games move to new places, and why does each sport need its own room?

James Naismith makes basketball at a YMCA school in Springfield
Charles Miller brings two soccer balls and a rule book home to Brazil
The Illinois High School Association begins
FIFA is founded in Paris on 21 May
The IHSA crowns its first boys wrestling state champions
Judo joins the Olympic Games in Tokyo
The IHSA holds its first girls wrestling state finals

title: Many Games, One Book

chapters.title: Games That Travel
chapters.bigQuestion: How did ball games move from one town to towns across the world?

story.title: A Ball With No Writing
story.kicker: An old ball rolls out of a gym closet, and a class wonders where games come from.
paragraphs: Mr. Reyes opens the gym closet. An old ball rolls out. It has no name on it. The leather is smooth and dark from many hands.
"Who made this game?" asks Nia. Mr. Reyes smiles. "Soccer rules were first written down in London in 1863," he says. "But people kicked balls long before that."
He points to a map on the wall. "Ships carried balls across oceans. Teachers carried rules to new schools. That is how a game moves."
Nia holds the ball up to the light. She thinks of all the towns it might have visited. Then she sets it back on the shelf.
story.think: What does a game need to move to a new town: a ball, a rule, or both?

lessons.title: Rubber Balls in Old Mexico
lessons.mainIdea: People in old Mexico played with rubber balls on stone courts over 3,000 years ago.
reading: People in Mexico and Central America played a ball game over 3,000 years ago. Their balls were made of *rubber*. Rubber comes from the milky sap of a tree.
Players used a long, narrow *ball court* with walls on each side. A huge stone court still stands at Chichén Itzá in Mexico. Two stone rings sit high on its walls.
Spanish visitors saw the game in the 1500s. Europe had no rubber balls then. The bouncing balls amazed the visitors.

words.d: a bouncy stuff made from the sap of certain trees
a long stone alley with walls where the old Mexican ball game was played

look.text: Picture a long stone alley in the sun. Tall walls rise on both sides. High on each wall is a round stone ring. It is the Great Ball Court at Chichén Itzá, in Mexico.
look.prompt: What part of this court tells you it was built for a ball game?

check.why: The balls were made of rubber from tree sap.

check.q: Where does a huge old stone ball court still stand?

check.q: Why were Spanish visitors amazed in the 1500s?

check.why: Europe had no rubber, so the bouncing balls were new to them.

lessons.title: Kick Ball in Old China
lessons.mainIdea: In old China, people played a kicking game called cuju more than 2,000 years ago.
reading: People in old China played a game called *cuju*. The name means "kick ball." It was played more than 2,000 years ago.
Soldiers played cuju to stay strong. Later, people at the emperor's palace played it too. The ball was made of leather.
China kept written records about cuju. FIFA is the world soccer group. It has called cuju the oldest kicking game with written history.

words.d: an old Chinese kicking game; the name means "kick ball"

look.text: Picture a palace yard in old China. People in long robes stand in a circle. A leather ball flies up from someone's foot. A writer at the side keeps notes about the game.

lessons.title: The Creator's Game
lessons.mainIdea: Native nations of North America played lacrosse long before Europeans came.
reading: Native nations of North America played a stick-and-ball game for hundreds of years. The Haudenosaunee, also called the Iroquois, are one of those nations.
French visitors saw the game in the 1600s. They gave it a French name, *lacrosse*. Many Haudenosaunee people call it the Creator's Game.
The Haudenosaunee still play today. They have their own national team. It plays against other countries in world contests.

words.d: a stick-and-ball game first played by Native nations of North America
a group of Native nations, also called the Iroquois

lessons.title: Rules Written in London
lessons.mainIdea: On 26 October 1863, clubs in London formed the Football Association to share one set of rules.
reading: Long ago, English schools each played football their own way. Some let players carry the ball. Others only let them kick it.
On 26 October 1863, club leaders met at a tavern in London. They formed the *Football Association*. They wrote one set of rules to share.
People shortened "association" to *soccer*. That is where the word comes from. In England, the game is still called football.

words.d: the group formed in London in 1863 to write shared football rules

lessons.title: Two Balls in a Suitcase
lessons.mainIdea: People who learned soccer in England carried the game to South America.
reading: British people living in Argentina started a soccer club in Buenos Aires in 1867. It was one of the first in South America.
Charles Miller was born in Brazil. He went to school in England and learned soccer there. In 1894 he came home with two balls and a rule book.
Soccer grew fast in South America. In 1930, Uruguay held the first World Cup. Uruguay won it, too.

words.d: the world soccer contest between countries, first held in Uruguay in 1930

lessons.title: Countries Join Hands
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904 so soccer groups from different countries could work together.
reading: By 1904, many countries had soccer groups. On 21 May 1904, seven of them met in Paris. They formed *FIFA*.
FIFA runs contests between countries, like the World Cup. Another group, the IFAB, keeps the Laws of the Game. The IFAB began in 1886.
FIFA started with seven members. Today it has 211 member associations from around the world.

words.d: the world soccer group, founded in Paris in 1904

sections.title: Hoops and Bats on the Move

lessons.title: Peach Baskets in Springfield
lessons.mainIdea: James Naismith made basketball in a YMCA gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in December 1891.
reading: James Naismith was a teacher from Canada. He worked at a *YMCA* school in Springfield, Massachusetts. In December 1891 he made up an indoor game for winter.
He nailed two peach baskets up high. He wrote 13 rules. His class had 18 students, so nine played on each side.
His rules were printed in the school paper in January 1892. YMCA teachers took the game to other gyms. It spread to many countries.

words.d: the Young Men's Christian Association, which ran the school where Naismith taught

lessons.title: Baseball Sails to Japan
lessons.mainIdea: An American teacher brought baseball to Japan in 1872, and a Chicago team toured the world in 1888.
reading: Horace Wilson was an American teacher in Tokyo, Japan. In 1872 he taught his students to play baseball. Japan later put him in its Baseball Hall of Fame.
In 1888, Albert Spalding led a *tour* with Chicago baseball players. They sailed around the world. They played games in Australia and Egypt.
Today baseball is a favorite game in Japan. High school teams there play in a big national contest every summer.

words.d: a long trip to many places, stopping to play or show something

chapters.title: A Mat Beside the Field
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do wrestling, boxing, fencing and judo each need a room of their own?

story.title: A Jacket Beside a Ball Bag
story.kicker: A folded white jacket hangs in a school hallway next to a bag of baseballs.
paragraphs: Two hooks hang by the gym door. A bag of baseballs sits on one hook. A folded white jacket and a belt hang on the other.
Sam touches the jacket. The cloth is thick and rough. "That is for the judo club," says Ms. Park. "Judo began at a school in Tokyo, Japan, in 1882."
"Where do they play?" asks Sam. "Not on the grass," says Ms. Park. "Judo uses a soft mat. Baseball uses a diamond. Each game has its own room."
Sam looks from the jacket to the ball bag. Two clubs share one hallway. They go to two very different floors. One floor is soft. One is grass and dirt.
story.think: Why might a judo club and a baseball team need different floors?

lessons.title: Wrestlers on a Tomb Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Painters in old Egypt showed hundreds of pairs of wrestlers on tomb walls about 4,000 years ago.
reading: Beni Hasan is a place along the Nile River in Egypt. Leaders were buried there in *tombs* cut into cliffs. The tombs are about 4,000 years old.
Painters covered some tomb walls with wrestlers. One wall shows hundreds of pairs, one after another. Each pair is painted in a different pose.
The paintings tell us wrestling is very, very old. Egyptians watched it long before soccer had rules.

words.d: a room or grave where a person is buried

lessons.title: A Wrestling School in Greece
lessons.mainIdea: Old Greeks built wrestling schools, and wrestling has been in the modern Olympics since 1896.
reading: Old Greeks trained in a building called a *palaestra*. It had an open yard with rooms around it. Wrestlers practiced there.
By tradition, wrestling joined the old Olympic Games at Olympia in 708 BCE. The modern Olympics began in Athens in 1896. Wrestling was there, too.
For a long time, only men wrestled at the Olympics. Women's wrestling was first held at the Athens Games in 2004.

words.d: an old Greek building where wrestlers trained

sections.title: A Square, a Strip, a Circle

lessons.title: A Roped Square
lessons.mainIdea: Boxing's Queensberry Rules of 1867 called for gloves and a square ring.
reading: In 1867, new boxing rules were printed in England. They were named for the Marquess of Queensberry. They are called the *Queensberry Rules*.
The rules called for padded gloves and rounds of three minutes. Matches were held in a *ring*. A boxing ring is really a square with ropes around it.
Boxing joined the Olympics in St. Louis in 1904. Women first boxed at the Olympics in London in 2012.

words.d: boxing rules printed in England in 1867
the roped square where boxing matches are held

look.text: The first rule says a match should be a fair stand-up boxing match in a ring 24 feet across, or as close to that size as possible.

lessons.title: A Long Thin Strip
lessons.mainIdea: Fencing uses a long, narrow floor called a strip, and it has been in every modern Olympics.
reading: Fencing is a sport with thin, blunt swords. Fencers stay on a long, narrow floor. It is called a *strip*, or a piste.
A strip is 14 meters long. That is longer than a school bus. It is less than 2 meters wide.
Fencing has been in every modern Olympics since 1896. Women first fenced at the Olympics in Paris in 1924.

words.d: the long, narrow floor used for fencing; also called a piste

lessons.title: A Clay Circle in Japan
lessons.mainIdea: Sumo wrestlers in Japan meet in a round clay ring called a dohyo.
reading: *Sumo* is a very old kind of wrestling from Japan. Sumo wrestlers meet in a round ring called a *dohyo*. It is made of packed clay.
Straw bales mark the edge of the circle. Before a bout, wrestlers toss salt into the ring. In Shinto tradition, salt makes a place clean.
Pro sumo holds six big tournaments each year. In pro sumo, only men may enter the ring. Women and girls wrestle in amateur sumo.

words.d: a very old kind of wrestling from Japan
the round clay ring used in sumo

lessons.title: A School Called the Kodokan
lessons.mainIdea: Kano Jigoro started judo at the Kodokan school in Tokyo in 1882.
reading: *Kano* Jigoro was a teacher in Japan. In 1882 he opened a school in Tokyo. It was called the Kodokan. It began in a small room at a Buddhist temple.
Kano named his art *judo*. The name means "gentle way." Students trained on straw mats called tatami. They wore thick cotton jackets.
A judo room is called a dojo. In many judo schools, students bow as they step onto the mat. They see the bow as a sign of respect.

words.d: Kano Jigoro, the teacher who started judo in Tokyo in 1882

lessons.title: From Tokyo to the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Judo joined the Olympics when Tokyo held the Games in 1964.
reading: In 1909, Kano became the first person from Asia on the *International Olympic Committee*. That group runs the Olympic Games.
Tokyo held the Olympics in 1964. Judo joined the Games that year. Men were the only judo players at first.
Women's judo became an Olympic medal sport in Barcelona in 1992. Taekwondo, from Korea, joined in 2000.

lessons.title: Wrestling Mats in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois high schools held a boys wrestling state meet in 1937 and a girls state meet in 2022.

School wrestlers meet on a thick, padded *mat*. The first IHSA boys state champions came in 1937.
Girls wrestled in Illinois before they had their own meet. Their first IHSA state finals came in 2022.
